attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful restatement of a past-tense observation about Facebook M.

contract.note: Taking 'never took off' to mean no broad availability or uptake is the ordinary reading, and it is not stretched either way. Separating the original service from M Suggestions is appropriate.

evidence.note: Contemporary Verge report: the human-powered M reached only about 2,000 Californians, the promised expansion never happened, and Facebook called it an experiment.
Facebook's own 2016 statement that the test was going well. It does not show broad uptake.

reviews.rationale: Contemporary reporting shows the original concierge M stayed a limited beta, with no expansion before it was shut down in January 2018. Facebook's upbeat 2016 statement is a company disclosure and does not show broad uptake.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The sentence also says the human involvement 'eventually leaked', meaning it was hidden at first. The normalised proposition drops this, so it commits the speaker to less than he said.

contract.note: The contract grades operational human involvement and checks the leak implication as a separate qualification. That is fair, but the verdict depends on whether the leak element is graded.

evidence.note: Launch-day Wired report: human trainers did tasks the software could not, so people were operationally involved. Facebook's own sources described this at launch.
Facebook's launch announcement said M was supervised by people. This supports human involvement but contradicts the claim that it only came out later through a leak.

reviews.rationale: The evidence supports that humans did operational work behind M's interface. It contradicts the claim that this 'eventually leaked': Facebook disclosed human trainers at launch in August 2015, although users could not tell which replies came from people.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the January 2018 date and the under-three-years span. 'Ended in sorrow' is rhetoric and rightly not graded.

contract.note: Dating launch from the August 2015 trial and cancellation from the January 2018 announcement or shutdown is ordinary. Either endpoint gives the same result.

evidence.note: Dated report shows Facebook announced M on 26 August 2015, as a limited release.
Wired, 8 January 2018: Facebook will shut M on 19 January, under three years after launch.

reviews.rationale: M launched in August 2015. Its cancellation was announced on 8 January 2018 and service ended on 19 January 2018. That is January 2018, about two and a half years after launch, so less than three years.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the causal 'so', the approximate count and the never-scaled assertion. 'Part of the problem' is kept in the contract as a contributing cause, not the sole cause.

contract.note: Expense as a material, not sole, constraint matches 'part of the problem'. Counting people given access is a fair reading of 'users'.

evidence.note: Verge 2017: because M was so resource-intensive, Facebook had not expanded it to the public. Qualitative support for the mechanism.
Tech Review 2017 reports limited access and, per the packet, about 10,000 users and prohibitive cost. The quoted excerpt shows only the limited access.
The Register reports a beta of about 2,000, which conflicts with the 10,000 figure. Facebook declined to give its reasons or spending.

reviews.rationale: Two of three parts hold. M was never released to the general public, and independent reports link this to its costly human staffing. The 'about 10,000 users' figure is disputed: one report gives roughly 10,000, another about 2,000, so the packet does not settle the count.
